title: ConfigMaps & Secrets: The Kubernetes Configuration Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets — how they store data, how env vars and volume mounts differ in update behavior, why base64 is encoding not encryption, and how to rotate config without breaking Pods. Covers immutability, subPath traps, projected volumes, RBAC, and encryption at rest.

chapters.title: Why Config Lives Outside the Image
points: Twelve-factor principle: config varies by deploy environment, code does not — bake code into the image, inject config at runtime
Anti-pattern: rebuilding a container image just to change a database URL couples release cadence to config cadence
ConfigMap = API object holding non-confidential key/value data; Secret = same shape but intended for sensitive data with extra handling
Both are namespaced objects — a Pod can only reference ConfigMaps/Secrets in its own namespace, never cross-namespace
Both live in etcd and are served by the API server; Pods never read them from disk on the node directly
Consumption modes: (1) container env vars, (2) files in a volume, (3) command-line args via env substitution, (4) Kubelet-read fields like imagePullSecrets
1 MiB hard size limit per ConfigMap and per Secret — enforced because etcd holds them entirely in memory and API server caches them
ConfigMap `data` holds UTF-8 strings; `binaryData` holds base64-encoded bytes for non-UTF-8 content (certs, tarballs, .p12 keystores)
Secret `data` is always base64-encoded on the wire; `stringData` is a write-only convenience field that the API server encodes into `data` for you
Naming rule: keys must match `[-._a-zA-Z0-9]+`; `..` alone and keys starting with `..` are rejected
Mental model: ConfigMap/Secret are just typed key/value blobs — all the interesting behavior comes from *how* a Pod consumes them

chapters.title: Anatomy of a ConfigMap
points: Minimal manifest: `apiVersion: v1`, `kind: ConfigMap`, `metadata.name`, then `data:` map of key to string value
Two content shapes: property-like keys (`LOG_LEVEL: debug`) and file-like keys (`nginx.conf: |` with a multi-line block scalar)
File-like keys matter because volume mounts turn each key into a filename — `app.properties` becomes a file named `app.properties`
`kubectl create configmap app --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug --from-literal=PORT=8080` for quick key/value pairs
`kubectl create configmap app --from-file=./nginx.conf` uses the basename as the key; `--from-file=conf=./nginx.conf` renames it
`--from-file=./configdir/` slurps every file in the directory into its own key; subdirectories are skipped, hidden files ignored
`--from-env-file=app.env` parses `KEY=value` lines into keys — the only form that makes each line a separate key rather than one file blob
YAML gotcha: unquoted `true`, `no`, `8080`, `3.10` are typed by YAML — ConfigMap `data` values must be strings, so quote them or the apply fails
`kubectl create cm x --from-file=y --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml` is the standard way to generate a manifest for GitOps
Kustomize `configMapGenerator` appends a content hash suffix to the name (`app-7d9f2k4b8c`) and rewrites references — this is the cleanest rollout mechanism
ConfigMaps have no schema and no validation — a typo in a key is silently accepted and only fails at Pod start or at app parse time

chapters.title: Anatomy of a Secret
points: Secret manifest mirrors ConfigMap but adds a `type` field that signals structure to controllers and kubelet
`Opaque` — the default, arbitrary user-defined key/value, no structural validation
`kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` — required key `.dockerconfigjson`; consumed via `imagePullSecrets`, read by the kubelet, never mounted
`kubernetes.io/tls` — required keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`; consumed by Ingress controllers and cert-manager
`kubernetes.io/basic-auth` (`username`, `password`), `kubernetes.io/ssh-auth` (`ssh-privatekey`), `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`
`bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token` — used for kubeadm node join flow, not application config
Typed Secrets are validated: creating a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret without `tls.key` is rejected at admission — use types to get free validation
`stringData` write path: `stringData.password: hunter2` is merged into `data` as base64 at write time; if a key exists in both, `stringData` wins
`kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=hunter2` shell-history leaks the value — prefer `--from-file=password=./pw.txt`
Since Kubernetes 1.24, creating a ServiceAccount no longer auto-creates a long-lived token Secret — Pods get projected, short-lived, audience-bound tokens instead
`kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` is the read path; anyone with `get secret` RBAC can do this

chapters.title: Base64 Is Not Encryption
points: Base64 is a binary-to-text *encoding*: it maps 3 bytes to 4 ASCII chars so arbitrary bytes survive JSON/YAML transport — it has no key and no secret
Reversal is one command with no credential: `echo aHVudGVyMg== | base64 -d` prints `hunter2`
Why Kubernetes uses it at all: Secret values may be raw binary (a DER cert, a keytab); JSON has no binary type, so encoding is mandatory
Consequence 1: a Secret manifest committed to git is a plaintext credential in git — the encoding buys zero protection
Consequence 2: by default Secrets are stored **unencrypted** in etcd; anyone with etcd disk access or an etcd backup reads every Secret
Real protection layer 1 — encryption at rest: `EncryptionConfiguration` on the API server with an `aescbc`/`secretbox`/`kms` provider for `resources: [secrets]`
KMS v2 provider is the production choice: envelope encryption, DEK cached in API server, KEK held in cloud KMS/HSM, supports key rotation without full rewrite
After enabling or rotating encryption you must rewrite existing objects: `kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -`
Real protection layer 2 — RBAC: `get`/`list`/`watch` on `secrets` is equivalent to reading the secret; `list` on a namespace leaks every Secret in it
Real protection layer 3 — external stores: External Secrets Operator, Vault Agent Injector, or Secrets Store CSI Driver keep the source of truth outside etcd
For git: SOPS or Sealed Secrets encrypt with a key the cluster holds; plain base64 in a repo is a finding in every security audit
Practical difference from ConfigMaps is thin: Secrets are not written to node disk in plaintext (tmpfs), are omitted from `kubectl describe`, and can be separately encrypted — that is the whole delta

chapters.title: Injecting as Environment Variables
points: Single key: `env: [{name: LOG_LEVEL, valueFrom: {configMapKeyRef: {name: app, key: LOG_LEVEL}}}]`
Secret equivalent uses `secretKeyRef` with the same `name`/`key` shape
Bulk import: `envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: app}}, {secretRef: {name: db}}]` maps every key to an env var of the same name
`envFrom` with `prefix: APP_` renames every imported key — useful to avoid collisions between two sources
Keys that are not valid env var names (e.g. `nginx.conf`) are **silently skipped** by `envFrom` and reported as an event, not an error
Precedence: explicit `env` entries override `envFrom` entries with the same name; later `envFrom` sources override earlier ones
`optional: true` lets the Pod start when the referenced ConfigMap/Secret or key is missing; default is `optional: false`
Missing required reference leaves the Pod in `CreateContainerConfigError` — check `kubectl describe pod`, not the container logs, which do not exist yet
Env vars support `$(VAR)` expansion inside `command` and `args` and inside later `env` values — escape a literal with `$$(...)`
**Env vars are resolved once, at container start.** Updating the ConfigMap does *not* change a running container's environment — ever
Env vars leak: they appear in `kubectl describe pod`, in crash dumps, in child processes, in `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and in many APM/error-reporting agents
Rule of thumb: env vars for small, stable, non-sensitive scalars; anything secret or reloadable belongs in a volume

chapters.title: Injecting as Volume Mounts
points: Declare a volume `{name: cfg, configMap: {name: app}}`, then `volumeMounts: [{name: cfg, mountPath: /etc/app}]`
Each key becomes a file at `mountPath/<key>`; the file content is the value, with no trailing newline added
`items` selects a subset and renames: `items: [{key: nginx.conf, path: conf.d/default.conf}]` — unlisted keys are not projected at all
`defaultMode: 0400` sets file permissions octal-wide; per-item `mode` overrides it — YAML needs `0400` written as `0400`, and it is decimal unless prefixed
`fsGroup` in the Pod securityContext, not the mount, controls group ownership — mode alone will not fix a permission-denied for a non-root user
Secret volumes are backed by **tmpfs** (memory), so secret bytes never touch the node's disk; ConfigMap volumes use the same emptyDir-like path but are not sensitive
The mount is **read-only** for ConfigMap/Secret volumes — an app that rewrites its own config file in place will fail
Mounting onto a non-empty directory (e.g. `/etc`) **shadows** the original contents for that container — mount into a dedicated dir and symlink, or use subPath deliberately
**Volume mounts update automatically.** The kubelet refreshes projected files, so a `kubectl edit configmap` reaches running Pods without a restart
Update latency = kubelet sync period (default 1 min) + ConfigMap cache TTL — worst case roughly 2× sync period; it is eventual, not instant
`configMapAndSecretChangeDetectionStrategy` on the kubelet controls this: `Watch` (default, fastest), `TTL`, or `Cache`
Volumes are the only mode that supports live reload, so any config an app should re-read at runtime must be a file

chapters.title: Atomic Updates and the Symlink Dance
points: The kubelet does **not** overwrite files in place — it writes a whole new version directory and flips a symlink, so readers never see a half-written file
On-disk layout: `..2024_01_15_10_30_00.123456/` holds the real files, `..data` is a symlink to that directory, and each key is a symlink to `..data/<key>`
`ls -la /etc/app` reveals this: `app.conf -> ..data/app.conf`. `ls` alone hides it
Update sequence: write new timestamped dir → create `..data_tmp` symlink → `rename()` it over `..data` (atomic on POSIX) → delete old dir
Because the swap is a rename of a directory symlink, the update is atomic *as a set* — you never see key A updated and key B stale
Consequence for inotify: watching the file path gives you no `IN_MODIFY` — the inode changed. Watch the **directory** for `IN_CREATE`/`IN_MOVED_TO` on `..data`
Libraries that get this wrong (naive `fsnotify` on the file) silently stop reloading after the first update — this is the classic 'reload works once' bug
Apps that `open()` the file once at boot and hold the descriptor keep reading the *old* inode forever — reopen by path on every reload
Reload strategies: signal-based (`nginx -s reload` from a sidecar), inotify in-process, or plain polling with a stat/hash comparison
Reloader / Stakater Reloader annotations (`configmap.reloader.stakater.com/reload`) restart the Deployment instead — coarse but foolproof
The `..` prefix on the internal names is why ConfigMap keys may not begin with `..` — it would collide with the machinery

chapters.title: The subPath Trap
points: `subPath: nginx.conf` mounts a *single* file into a directory without shadowing that directory's other contents — e.g. into `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`
This is the standard workaround for 'I need one file in a directory that already has files'
**The trap: subPath mounts never receive updates.** The kubelet resolves the subPath once at container start and bind-mounts that specific file
Mechanism: a subPath bind-mount points at the inode inside the current timestamped directory; when the symlink flips, the bind-mount still points at the old, now-unlinked inode
Symptom: `kubectl exec` shows the old content forever, while a sibling non-subPath mount of the same ConfigMap shows the new content — deeply confusing during an incident
This is documented behavior, not a bug: 'a container using a ConfigMap as a subPath volume will not receive ConfigMap updates'
Fix A — mount the whole volume into a dedicated directory and point the app at `/etc/app-config/nginx.conf`
Fix B — mount into a scratch dir and symlink or copy into place from an initContainer (breaks live reload but is explicit)
Fix C — use `subPathExpr` with the downward API for per-Pod paths (`subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)`) — still no updates, but avoids hardcoding
Fix D — accept it and force a rollout on change (hash-suffixed ConfigMap names or a pod-template annotation)
Second trap: `subPath` into an existing file requires the file to already exist in the image, otherwise the kubelet creates a *directory* with that name and the app fails to parse it
Third trap: `subPath` with a value that escapes the volume (`../`) is rejected — the kubelet validates against path traversal

chapters.title: Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
points: Set `immutable: true` on a ConfigMap or Secret; stable since Kubernetes 1.21
Once set, `data`, `binaryData`, and `stringData` can never change — and `immutable` itself cannot be flipped back to false
Only `metadata` (labels, annotations) stays mutable; to change content you delete and recreate, or create a new name
Benefit 1 — safety: no accidental `kubectl edit` silently reconfiguring hundreds of running Pods across a cluster
Benefit 2 — performance: the kubelet **closes the watch** on immutable objects after the first read, eliminating per-Pod watch load on the API server
The performance win is the real motivation at scale: a 5,000-node cluster with a shared ConfigMap otherwise holds thousands of open watches
Immutability pairs naturally with content-hash naming (`app-config-7d9f2k4b`) so a change is always a new object plus a Deployment rollout
Trade-off: you lose live reload entirely — every change is a Pod restart, so this suits config where a rollout is desired anyway
Migration path: add `immutable: true` to existing objects with `kubectl patch cm app -p '{"immutable":true}'` — irreversible, so verify first
Garbage collection is on you: hash-named immutable objects accumulate; prune old ones with a label selector and a retention policy
Immutable objects still count against the 1 MiB limit and against namespace resource quotas

chapters.title: Env vs Volume: The Comparison Table
points: Live updates — env: never; volume: yes, within ~1–2 kubelet sync periods; volume+subPath: never
App code changes needed — env: none, `os.Getenv` just works; volume: must read and optionally watch a file
Exposure surface — env: visible in `describe pod`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, crash dumps, child processes; volume: file with settable mode, readable only by the process
Data shape — env: flat strings only; volume: full files, so JSON/YAML/PEM/binary all work
Size — env: bounded by ARG_MAX (~2 MB total env block, plus a 1 MiB object limit); volume: 1 MiB object limit, no ARG_MAX pressure
Startup failure mode — env: `CreateContainerConfigError` before the container starts; volume: same for a missing object, but a missing *key* with `items` also blocks
Legacy app fit — env: perfect for twelve-factor apps; volume: required for apps that only read config files (nginx, postgres, java properties)
Ordering/precedence — env: explicit `env` beats `envFrom`, later sources beat earlier; volume: `items` fully replaces the default key set
Rotation story — env: rotate by rolling the Deployment; volume: rotate in place if the app reloads, otherwise still roll
Recommendation: secrets → volume mount with mode 0400 on tmpfs; feature flags and non-sensitive scalars → env; anything an operator will tweak at 3 a.m. → volume
Hybrid is normal: `envFrom` a ConfigMap for scalars *and* mount a Secret volume for credentials in the same container

chapters.title: Rotation Without Downtime
points: Three rotation strategies: (1) mutate in place and rely on volume reload, (2) new hash-named object plus rollout, (3) external secret manager with its own refresh loop
Strategy 1 — in-place: `kubectl apply` the new ConfigMap; volume-mounted files update; app reloads via inotify or SIGHUP. No rollout, no downtime, but requires app support
Strategy 2 — hash-named: Kustomize `configMapGenerator`/`secretGenerator` emits `app-<hash>`, rewrites all references, and the Pod template change triggers a normal RollingUpdate
Strategy 2 without Kustomize: put a checksum in the Pod template annotation — Helm's `checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/cm.yaml") . | sha256sum }}`
Why the annotation is needed: editing a ConfigMap does not change the Deployment spec, so the Deployment controller sees nothing to roll

Strategy 3 — External Secrets Operator syncs from Vault/AWS Secrets Manager into a k8s Secret on a `refreshInterval`; Secrets Store CSI Driver mounts directly and can rotate with `enableSecretRotation`
Credential rotation needs **overlap**: provision the new credential, deploy config that accepts both old and new, drain, then revoke the old one
Never revoke the old credential before every Pod has picked up the new one — check rollout status, not just the ConfigMap version
For TLS certs, cert-manager renews the Secret in place; Ingress controllers watch and reload, but apps mounting the cert need their own reload path
Auditing rotation: `kubectl rollout history`, plus the object's `metadata.resourceVersion` and `metadata.managedFields` to see who last wrote it
Blast radius control: one Secret per credential, not one mega-Secret — rotating a shared blob restarts every consumer of every key in it

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging
points: Mistake: expecting env vars to update on ConfigMap change. They never do. Verify with `kubectl exec -- env` versus `kubectl get cm -o yaml`
Mistake: `subPath` plus an edited ConfigMap, then hours lost. Check `ls -la` in the mount dir — no `..data` symlink means it is a subPath bind-mount
Mistake: mounting into `/etc` or `/app` and wiping the image's own files. Always mount into a dedicated path
Mistake: committing base64 Secrets to git and calling it secured. Use SOPS, Sealed Secrets, or an external store
Mistake: unquoted YAML values — `LOG_LEVEL: no` becomes boolean false and the apply is rejected with 'cannot unmarshal !!bool into string'
Mistake: keys with dots or dashes in `envFrom` are silently dropped as invalid env names — check Pod events for `InvalidVariableNames`
Mistake: trailing newline from `--from-file` or a heredoc breaking a token comparison — use `printf %s` or `tr -d '\n'` when creating the Secret
Mistake: a non-root container cannot read a mode-0400 file owned by root — set `fsGroup` in the Pod securityContext
Mistake: forgetting the namespace — a Pod cannot reference a ConfigMap in another namespace; the Pod hangs in `CreateContainerConfigError`

Debug checklist: `kubectl describe pod` for events → `kubectl get cm/secret -o yaml` for content → `kubectl exec -- ls -la <mountPath>` for the symlink layout → `kubectl exec -- cat <file>` for actual content → `kubectl exec -- env` for env state
Blast radius: a bad ConfigMap edit reaches every Pod mounting it within ~2 minutes, with no rollout and no rollback — this is the strongest argument for immutable, hash-named objects
Quota and limits: `count/configmaps` and `count/secrets` ResourceQuotas exist; hitting the 1 MiB limit yields 'Request entity too large' from the API server

chapters.title: Beyond the Basics: Projected Volumes and External Stores
points: `projected` volumes combine multiple sources — ConfigMaps, Secrets, downwardAPI, and serviceAccountToken — into one directory
Use case: one `/etc/config` directory assembled from a base ConfigMap, an environment overlay, and a Secret, with no mount-point juggling
`serviceAccountToken` projection gives short-lived, audience-scoped, auto-rotated tokens — the modern replacement for static ServiceAccount token Secrets
Token projection fields: `audience`, `expirationSeconds` (min 600), `path`; the kubelet rotates at 80% of lifetime, so apps must reread the file
Secrets Store CSI Driver mounts from Vault/AWS/Azure/GCP directly into the Pod, optionally syncing a k8s Secret as a mirror
External Secrets Operator uses a CRD (`ExternalSecret` + `SecretStore`) to pull into a native Secret on an interval — better ecosystem compatibility, weaker isolation
Compare: CSI driver keeps secrets out of etcd entirely; ESO puts them in etcd but works with every existing consumer
`imagePullSecrets` is a special path — read by the kubelet against the registry, never exposed to the container
Downward API volumes project Pod metadata (labels, annotations, resource limits) as files — same atomic-symlink update mechanics as ConfigMaps
Admission-time alternatives: Vault Agent Injector and similar mutating webhooks add a sidecar that writes rendered templates to a shared emptyDir
Choosing: start with ConfigMap + Secret; move to an external store when you need audit logs, dynamic credentials, or secrets that must never enter etcd

chapters.title: Summary: Rules That Hold
points: ConfigMaps and Secrets are the same object shape; Secrets add tmpfs backing, `describe` redaction, typed validation, and optional encryption at rest
Base64 is encoding, not encryption — protection comes from RBAC, encryption at rest (KMS v2), and keeping plaintext out of git
Env vars are frozen at container start; volume mounts update live; subPath mounts never update. Memorize these three
Volume updates are atomic via a `..data` symlink flip — watch the directory, not the file, and reopen by path
Immutable objects buy safety and a large API-server watch-load reduction, at the cost of live reload — pair with hash-named objects
A ConfigMap edit alone never triggers a rollout: use a content hash in the name or a checksum annotation on the Pod template
Rotate with overlap — new credential valid before old one is revoked, and confirm rollout completion before revoking
Mount into dedicated directories; never mount over `/etc` and never expect a read-only mount to be writable
Prefer file mounts for secrets (mode 0400, tmpfs, fsGroup set) over env vars, which leak into `/proc`, dumps, and child processes
Split by blast radius: one Secret per credential, one ConfigMap per concern — shared blobs turn one rotation into a cluster-wide restart
Debug order: `describe pod` events → object YAML → `ls -la` the mount → `cat` the file → `env` in the container
Graduate to projected volumes, CSI drivers, or an external secret manager when you need rotation guarantees, audit trails, or secrets that never enter etcd
